Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. However, pin names alone do not tell the whole story. Always check the IC datasheet to confirm each pin’s function and recommended connections. During PCB layout , pay particular attention to switching nodes, feedback paths, and grounding. Proper component placement and routing can help reduce noise, improve power integrity, and ensure stable operation. Whether you’re designing a simple power supply or a more complex DC-DC converter, understanding these pins is an important step toward reliable PCB design.
